query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor microalloying addition of niobium (Nb) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will refine its lamellar microstructure through in-situ precipitation and grain-boundary pinning, leading to enhanced resistance to high-temperature creep, improved corrosion stability, and a better strength–ductility balance under extreme operating conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure that currently offers good strength and plasticity but falls short in long-term high-temperature performance and corrosion resistance required for aerospace fasteners.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small amount (approximately 2–3 atomic percent) of Nb during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: Test conditions involve exposure to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (including creep at room and moderately elevated temperatures), and corrosive environments typical for aerospace fasteners.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined lamellar structure characterized by a distribution of nano-scale Nb-rich precipitates at grain boundaries and within the lamellae.
generation.mechanism: The introduced Nb is expected to segregate at grain boundaries and form fine precipitates that inhibit grain growth and lamellar coarsening during service. This pinning effect stabilizes the microstructure at high temperatures, reduces creep deformation, and may aid in the formation or stabilization of a protective passive film, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the Nb-modified alloy is predicted to exhibit higher yield strength, lower creep rate, and improved corrosion resistance while maintaining an acceptable degree of ductility.
generation.baseline: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with its current lamellar microstructure, which, despite good strength and ductility, exhibits performance limitations under extended high-temperature and corrosive exposures.
generation.boundary: The performance enhancement is anticipated when Nb content is kept at a microalloying level (around 2–3 at.%), ensuring that no brittle intermetallic phases form. The improvements depend on achieving a uniform dispersion of Nb during standard alloy fabrication methods. Exceeding the optimal range or using incompatible processing conditions could negate benefits.
generation.uncertainty: Precise Nb concentration and processing parameters required to optimize the enhanced properties remain uncertain. Additionally, the balance between increased strength and any unintended reduction in ductility under all extreme conditions must be carefully verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples: one set with approximately 2–3 at.% Nb added and a control set without Nb. Subject both sets to high-temperature creep tests, cyclic thermal loading to simulate extreme temperature fluctuations, and standardized corrosion tests in environments representative of aerospace applications. Use transmission and scanning electron microscopy (TEM/SEM) to evaluate the microstructural features such as precipitate distribution and lamellar refinement.
measurements: Creep rate (under defined load and temperature conditions)
Corrosion current density or mass loss in corrosion tests
Microstructural characterization (grain size, precipitate size and distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if Nb microalloying does not yield statistically significant improvements in yield strength, creep resistance (i.e., a noticeably lower creep rate), and corrosion resistance relative to the control, or if the addition of Nb causes a substantial decrease in ductility.
